analysis.one_liner: Abolishes the federal agency that enforces gun, alcohol, tobacco, and explosives laws.
analysis.headline: A one-page bill to eliminate the ATF was introduced in January 2025 with 34 Republican cosponsors, sent to the House Judiciary Committee, and has had no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: H.R. 221 would erase the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives — the federal agency that licenses gun dealers, traces crime guns, enforces laws against straw purchasing and trafficking, permits commercial explosives, and collects federal alcohol and tobacco taxes. The bill is a single sentence and contains no plan for moving those jobs to another agency. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Firearm manufacturers and dealers, who would be freed from dealer licensing, inspections, crime-gun tracing, and enforcement of trafficking laws. Explosives users would lose federal permitting oversight. People who want federal gun laws left unenforced would also get what they want.

how_it_helps.text: The bill's entire text is one sentence abolishing the ATF, with no provision transferring its duties elsewhere.

The ATF is the agency that issues federal firearms licenses, inspects dealers, traces guns used in crimes, and enforces laws against illegal gun sales and trafficking; abolishing it removes that enforcement.

The ATF also permits and regulates commercial explosives and collects federal excise taxes on alcohol and tobacco; abolishing it ends that regulatory and collection apparatus until Congress creates a replacement.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people bear the cost: less enforcement against illegal gun trafficking means more crime guns reaching streets, and a gap in tax collection and licensing for alcohol, tobacco, and explosives until new arrangements are made.

drawbacks.text: The bill has no transition plan: abolishing the agency in one sentence would leave unassigned the ATF's statutory jobs of licensing firearms dealers, tracing crime guns, permitting explosives, and collecting federal alcohol and tobacco taxes.
Ending ATF dealer inspections and gun tracing would remove the main federal tools for catching illegal gun trafficking, which affects public safety in communities experiencing gun crime.
Supporters argue the ATF has overreached in regulating firearms and should not exist; the bill's answer is outright elimination rather than restructuring or narrowing the agency's authority.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is ideological: removing an agency some gun-rights supporters see as an enemy of gun ownership. The costs are concrete: an enforcement, licensing, and tax-collection agency would disappear with nothing set up to replace it, and no committee has examined how those gaps would be filled. A one-sentence bill offers no way to weigh them.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee in January 2025, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Rep. Eric Burlison introduced the Abolish the ATF Act on January 7, 2025, with eight original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No further action — no markup, no committee vote, no floor action — appears in the bill's action history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never left committee, nothing changed: the ATF continues to operate, license dealers, and enforce federal firearms laws, and the gun industry remains subject to its oversight.

for.name: Rep. Lauren Boebert and seven other original cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 7, 2025 and has taken no action since — no markup, no vote, no report.

sides.party_line_note: All 35 sponsors and cosponsors are Republicans and no Democrat has joined; the bill sits in a committee where it has drawn no action from either party.

industries.note: The ATF licenses and inspects gun dealers, traces crime guns, and enforces laws against straw purchasing and trafficking. Abolishing it would free the industry from that oversight, with the cost falling on communities affected by illegal gun trafficking.

The ATF issues federal permits to alcohol and tobacco businesses and collects their excise taxes. Abolition would cut permit paperwork but leave tax collection and industry oversight in limbo until a replacement is set up.
The ATF issues federal permits for storing and using explosives in mining, construction, and fireworks. Ending that licensing removes a safety check on a hazardous industry at the public's expense.

analysis.trajectory: One-sentence abolition bills of this kind almost never receive a committee markup, and this one has had no activity in months. The realistic path is that it dies at the end of this Congress without a vote, unless it is attached to a larger bill.
